source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 3 (PDF 51-93, printed 48-90); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 3 (Cells and Subcellular Organelles), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.
3.1 Cells: the basic unit of life

blocks.prompt: 1 How many basic properties of life are shown by all living organisms?
blocks.explanation: All living organisms show seven basic properties: movement, respiration, homeostasis, growth, reproduction, excretion and nutrition (3.1).

book_ref.quote: all living organisms show the seven basic properties of life

blocks.prompt: 2 In amoebas and bacteria, the functions necessary for life are carried out by:
blocks.explanation: In unicellular organisms like amoebas and bacteria, a single cell carries out all the functions necessary for life (3.1).

book_ref.quote: a single cell carries out all the functions necessary for life

blocks.prompt: 3 During respiration, cells break glucose to release:
blocks.explanation: Respiration breaks glucose to release ATP, the energy currency that powers cellular activities (3.1).

book_ref.quote: This process breaks glucose to release ATP

blocks.prompt: 4 Gametes for sexual reproduction are produced by:
blocks.explanation: Mitosis produces identical daughter cells for growth and repair, while meiosis creates gametes (3.1).

book_ref.quote: while meiosis creates gametes for sexual reproduction

blocks.prompt: 5 Cells remove their waste products and prevent toxic buildup through:
blocks.explanation: Excretion: cells remove waste products through diffusion and active transport, preventing toxic buildup (3.1).

book_ref.quote: Cells remove waste products through diffusion and active transport

blocks.prompt: 6 Cells maintain a stable internal environment (homeostasis) by:

options.text: regulating the movement of substances across their membranes

blocks.explanation: Homeostasis: cells regulate the movement of substances across their membranes to keep the internal environment stable (3.1).

book_ref.quote: by regulating the movement of substances across their membranes

blocks.prompt: 7 In 1665, Robert Hooke observed "many little boxes" in a thin slice of:
blocks.explanation: Hooke examined a thin slice of cork of oak tree and saw that it was made of many little boxes (3.2).

book_ref.quote: examined a thin slice of cork of oak tree under microscope

blocks.prompt: 8 Robert Hooke named the compartments he saw in plant parts as:
blocks.explanation: Hooke concluded that parts of plants were made of compartments and named them "cellulae" (3.2).

book_ref.quote: Hooke named these compartments as

blocks.prompt: 9 Anton van Leeuwenhoek observed living cells in pond water and called them:
blocks.explanation: In 1673 Leeuwenhoek made a better microscope, observed living cells in pond water and called them animalcules (3.2).

book_ref.quote: observed living cells in pond water

blocks.prompt: 10 The nucleus in the cell was discovered in 1831 by:
blocks.explanation: In 1831 the British botanist Robert Brown discovered the nucleus in the cell (3.2).

book_ref.quote: in 1831 the British botanist Robert Brown discovered nucleus in the cell

blocks.prompt: 11 The German botanist who concluded in 1838 that all plants are composed of cells was:
blocks.explanation: In 1838 Matthias Schleiden concluded that all plants were composed of cells; the next year Schwann said the same for animals (3.2).

book_ref.quote: He concluded that all plants were composed of cells

blocks.prompt: 12 Theodor Schwann, who concluded that animals are composed of cells, was a:
blocks.explanation: The German zoologist Theodor Schwann concluded for animals what Schleiden had concluded for plants (3.2).

book_ref.quote: the German zoologist Theodor Schwann concluded the same for animals

blocks.prompt: 13 The German physician who observed that all cells come from other cells was:
blocks.explanation: Rudolf Virchow observed that all cells come from other cells (omnis cellula e cellula). The book's year 1885 is a misprint; he stated it in 1855 (3.2).

book_ref.quote: observed that all cells come from other cells

blocks.prompt: 14 Experimental proof that cells come from other cells was provided in 1862 by:
blocks.explanation: In 1862 Louis Pasteur provided the experimental proof that all cells come from other cells (3.2).

book_ref.quote: Louis Pasteur provided the experimental proof of this idea

blocks.prompt: 15 Which statement is one of the three points of the cell theory?

options.text: All cells contain a cell wall
Cells are the basic units of structure and function in an organism

blocks.explanation: The cell theory says: all organisms are made of cells; cells are the basic units of structure and function; cells come only from pre-existing cells (3.2).

book_ref.quote: Cells are the basic units of structure and function in an organism.

blocks.prompt: 16 Viruses are an exception to the cell theory because they:

options.text: are made of many nuclei in one cytoplasm
are not made of cells and need a host cell to replicate

blocks.explanation: Viruses are not made of cells, cannot carry out life processes independently and require a host cell to replicate (3.2).

book_ref.quote: They require a host cell to replicate

blocks.prompt: 17 Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own DNA and replicate independently. This suggests that they:

options.text: may have originated from free-living prokaryotic cells
are formed by fusion of vacuoles

blocks.explanation: Their own DNA and independent replication suggest that these organelles may have originated from free-living prokaryotic cells (3.2).

book_ref.quote: may have originated from free-living prokaryotic cells

blocks.prompt: 18 Vertebrate muscle cells (myocytes) challenge the concept of a single cell as the basic unit because they:
blocks.explanation: Myocytes can fuse to form multinucleated fibres, challenging the idea of a single cell as the basic unit in complex tissues (3.2).

book_ref.quote: can fuse to form multinucleated fibres

blocks.prompt: 19 Live-cell imaging and genetic studies validate which principle of the cell theory?

options.text: Cells are made of only proteins
All cells originate from pre-existing cells

blocks.explanation: These techniques track how cells replicate and give rise to new cells, validating that all cells originate from pre-existing cells (3.2).

book_ref.quote: techniques like live-cell imaging and genetic studies

blocks.prompt: 20 The technique that reveals that cells share common genetic material and metabolic pathways is:
blocks.explanation: DNA sequencing shows that cells share common genetic material and metabolic pathways, supporting the cell as the fundamental unit of life (3.2).

book_ref.quote: Techniques like DNA sequencing reveal that cells share common genetic material

blocks.prompt: 21 The technique of using microscopes to observe objects too small for the naked eye is called:
blocks.explanation: Microscopy is the technique of using microscopes to observe and study objects too small to be seen with the naked eye (3.3).

book_ref.quote: Microscopy is the technique of using microscopes to observe and study objects

blocks.prompt: 22 The total magnification of a microscope is determined by:

options.text: adding the magnifications of all its lenses
multiplying the magnifications of all its lenses
dividing the resolution by the magnification

blocks.explanation: Total magnification is found by multiplying the magnification of all lenses (3.3).

book_ref.quote: Total magnification in a microscope is determined by multiplying the magnification of all lenses

blocks.prompt: 23 A microscope's ability to distinguish between two points that are close together on an object is called its:
blocks.explanation: Resolution is the ability to distinguish two close points; the greater the resolution, the finer the detail seen (3.3).

book_ref.quote: ability to distinguish between two points that are close together on an object

blocks.prompt: 24 The resolution of the naked human eye is about:
blocks.explanation: The naked human eye resolves about 0.1 mm, while a light microscope resolves details down to about 250 nm (3.3).

book_ref.quote: The naked human eye has a resolution of about 0.1 mm

blocks.prompt: 25 In a light microscope, after passing through the object, light passes through:
blocks.explanation: Light passes through the object and then through two glass lenses; one enlarges the image and the second magnifies it more (3.3).

book_ref.quote: Light passes through object and then through two glass lenses

blocks.prompt: 26 The magnification of a light microscope, as given in the chapter, is about:
blocks.explanation: The magnification of a light microscope is 1500X, i.e. it can magnify objects about 1500 times (3.3).

book_ref.quote: The magnification of a light microscope is 1500X

blocks.prompt: 27 A light microscope cannot distinguish objects smaller than:
blocks.explanation: The resolving power of a light microscope is 0.2 µm (1 µm = 1/1000 mm) (3.3).

book_ref.quote: the light microscope cannot distinguish objects smaller than 0.2 µm

blocks.prompt: 28 Cell components seen under a light microscope are coloured with special stains. A drawback of staining is that it:
blocks.explanation: Cells are generally transparent, so stains (coloured chemicals) are used; staining, however, usually kills the cells (3.3).

book_ref.quote: Staining, however, usually kills the cells.

blocks.prompt: 29 In an electron microscope, the electron beam is focused by:
blocks.explanation: Magnetic lenses focus the electron beam on a screen or photographic film to make a much enlarged image (3.3).

book_ref.quote: Magnetic lenses focus the electron beam on a screen or photographic film

blocks.prompt: 30 An electron microscope can clearly show objects as small as:
blocks.explanation: The electron microscope can clearly show objects as small as 0.2 nanometre; 1 nm = 1/1000,000 mm (3.3).

book_ref.quote: It can clearly show objects as small as 0.2 nanometre (nm)

blocks.prompt: 31 An electron microscope cannot be used for viewing living material because:

options.text: of the methods needed to prepare the specimens
its resolution is lower than the eye

blocks.explanation: Electron microscopes cannot view living material because of the methods needed to prepare the specimens (3.3).

book_ref.quote: electron microscope cannot be used for viewing living material

blocks.prompt: 32 A Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) can magnify objects up to:
blocks.explanation: TEM transmits electrons through a very thin specimen and can magnify up to 250,000 times (3.3).

book_ref.quote: It can magnify objects up to 250,000 times.

blocks.prompt: 33 In a Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM), the image is made when the electron beam:

options.text: passes through a very thin specimen
is reflected from the metal coating of the surface

blocks.explanation: SEM studies surfaces: the surface is coated with metal, the electron beam is reflected from it and makes an enlarged image; SEMs magnify up to 100,000 times (3.3).

book_ref.quote: is used to study the details of surfaces of cells or any other objects

blocks.prompt: 34 Which statement is true for the electron microscope compared with the light microscope?

options.text: Both live and dead specimens can be seen
The image is seen through the ocular lens

blocks.explanation: For the electron microscope, specimen preparation takes several days and only dead, dried specimens are seen (3.3).

book_ref.quote: Specimen preparation takes several days

blocks.prompt: 35 Yeast and Euglena are examples of:
blocks.explanation: All bacteria are prokaryotes; yeast and Euglena are unicellular eukaryotes; plants and animals are multicellular eukaryotes (3.4).

book_ref.quote: Yeast and Euglena are examples of unicellular eukaryotes

blocks.prompt: 36 When the cell wall is removed by cell wall degrading enzymes, the remaining part of the cell is called:
blocks.explanation: Removing the cell wall with cell wall degrading enzymes leaves the protoplast (3.4).

book_ref.quote: the remaining components of the cell are called a protoplast

blocks.prompt: 37 The primary cell wall is composed of the polysaccharides:
blocks.explanation: The primary wall is composed of cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin, with many proteins (3.4).

book_ref.quote: It is composed of polysaccharides i.e. cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin

blocks.prompt: 38 In the primary wall, the cellulose microfibrils are aligned at all angles and are held together by:
blocks.explanation: The cellulose microfibrils of the primary wall are aligned at all angles and held together by hydrogen bonds (3.4).

book_ref.quote: are held together by hydrogen bonds

blocks.prompt: 39 The middle lamella contains:
blocks.explanation: The middle lamella is a gelatinous layer that contains magnesium and calcium pectates (salts of pectic acid) (3.4).

book_ref.quote: It contains magnesium and calcium pectates

blocks.prompt: 40 The middle lamella is formed from:
blocks.explanation: The middle lamella is laid first, formed from the cell plate during cytokinesis; the primary wall then expands inside it (3.4).

book_ref.quote: formed from the cell plate during cytokinesis

blocks.prompt: 41 The secondary cell wall is more rigid than the primary wall due to the presence of:
blocks.explanation: Secondary walls contain lignin, cellulose and hemicellulose; lignin makes them more rigid than the primary wall (3.4).

book_ref.quote: Due to the presence of lignin, secondary wall is more rigid than the primary wall

blocks.prompt: 42 Plasmodesmata are formed during cell division when:

options.text: lysosomes rupture in the cell plate
the nuclear envelope fuses with the wall
parts of the endoplasmic reticulum get trapped in the new cell wall

blocks.explanation: Plasmodesmata form when parts of the ER of the parent cell get trapped in the new cell wall (3.4).

book_ref.quote: when parts of the endoplasmic reticulum of the parent cell get trapped in the new cell wall

blocks.prompt: 43 The cell wall of fungi is composed of:
blocks.explanation: The fungal cell wall is made of chitin, the same carbohydrate that strengthens insect exoskeletons (3.4).

book_ref.quote: The cell wall of fungi is composed of chitin

blocks.prompt: 44 Diatoms show high growth rates because their cell walls are made from:

options.text: silicic acid (silica), which needs less energy

blocks.explanation: Diatoms synthesize cell walls from silicic acid; silica walls need less energy, so diatoms grow faster (3.4).

book_ref.quote: synthesize their cell walls from silicic acid

blocks.prompt: 45 Which cell wall contains no peptidoglycan?
blocks.explanation: Bacteria and cyanobacteria have peptidoglycan walls; archaebacteria have different polysaccharides and proteins, with no peptidoglycan (3.4).

book_ref.quote: The cell wall of archaebacteria is composed of different polysaccharides and proteins

blocks.prompt: 46 The fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane was proposed in 1972 by:
blocks.explanation: The fluid mosaic model was proposed by S.J. Singer and Garth Nicolson in 1972 (3.4).

book_ref.quote: It was proposed by two American biologists S.J. Singer and Garth Nicolson in 1972

blocks.prompt: 47 In the lipid bilayer of the plasma membrane:

options.text: the hydrophobic tails point inwards and the hydrophilic phosphate groups face outwards
both heads and tails face the cytoplasm
the tails face the extracellular environment

blocks.explanation: The hydrophobic lipid tails are oriented inwards and the hydrophilic phosphate groups face the cytoplasm or the extracellular environment (3.4).

book_ref.quote: the hydrophobic lipid tails are oriented inwards

blocks.prompt: 48 In eukaryotic plasma membranes, cholesterol molecules wedged into the bilayer:

options.text: make the membrane impermeable to water
keep the membrane fluid at low temperatures

blocks.explanation: Cholesterol molecules wedged into the phospholipid bilayer keep the fluidity of the membrane at low temperatures (3.4).

book_ref.quote: They keep the fluidity of membrane at low temperatures

blocks.prompt: 49 The glycolipids and glycoproteins on the outer surface of the plasma membrane, collectively called glycocalyx, function as:
blocks.explanation: The glycocalyx acts as cell identification marks recognized by other cells; it varies between species, individuals and cell types (3.4).

book_ref.quote: function as cell identification marks that are recognized by other cells

blocks.prompt: 50 According to the table of membrane composition, the membrane with the highest percentage of protein by weight is:

options.text: the human red blood cell membrane (49%)

blocks.explanation: The table gives protein: red blood cell 49, outer mitochondrial 52, inner mitochondrial 76, bacteria 75 percent by weight (3.4).

book_ref.quote: Mitochondria (inner membrane)

blocks.prompt: 51 Which molecules pass freely across the plasma membrane?
blocks.explanation: Small molecules such as oxygen, carbon dioxide and water pass freely, but the passage of amino acids and sugars is carefully regulated (3.4).

book_ref.quote: the passage of larger molecules, such as amino acids and sugars, is carefully regulated

blocks.prompt: 52 The technique used to determine the atomic structure of membrane proteins is:
blocks.explanation: X-ray crystallography is used to determine the atomic structure of membrane proteins (3.4).

book_ref.quote: is used to determine the atomic structure of membrane proteins

blocks.prompt: 53 Bleaching a fluorescently labelled region of the membrane with a laser and watching fluorescence return is the technique of:
blocks.explanation: FRAP studies the mobility of membrane proteins and lipids: unbleached molecules moving into the bleached area restore fluorescence (3.4).

book_ref.quote: is used to study the mobility and dynamics of membrane proteins and lipids

blocks.prompt: 54 Lipidomics, the comprehensive analysis of membrane lipids, uses techniques like:
blocks.explanation: Lipidomics analyses the lipids of the cell membrane using techniques like mass spectrometry (3.4).

book_ref.quote: comprehensive analysis of lipids in the cell membrane

blocks.prompt: 55 Plasma membrane proteins that bind messenger molecules such as hormones and pass the signal inside are:
blocks.explanation: Some membrane proteins act as receptors that bind messenger molecules (e.g. hormones) and transmit signals to the interior (3.4).

book_ref.quote: which bind messenger molecules (e.g. hormones)

blocks.prompt: 56 The aqueous ground substance of the cytoplasm is called:
blocks.explanation: The cytoplasm consists of an aqueous ground substance, the cytosol, containing organelles and inclusions (3.4).

book_ref.quote: It consists of an aqueous ground substance, known as cytosol

blocks.prompt: 57 Glycolysis, the breakdown of glucose during aerobic respiration, takes place in the:
blocks.explanation: The cytoplasm is the site of many metabolic reactions, for example glycolysis (3.4).

book_ref.quote: acts as the site for various biochemical (metabolic) reactions

blocks.prompt: 58 The spherical nucleus typically occupies about what part of a eukaryotic cell's volume?
blocks.explanation: The nucleus typically occupies about 10 percent of a eukaryotic cell's volume (3.4).

book_ref.quote: The spherical nucleus typically occupies about 10 percent of a eukaryotic

blocks.prompt: 59 The perinuclear space between the two layers of the nuclear envelope is connected with the:
blocks.explanation: The space between the double layers (perinuclear space) is connected with the rough endoplasmic reticulum (3.4).

book_ref.quote: The space between the double layers is called the perinuclear space

blocks.prompt: 60 The protein lining on the inner side of the nuclear envelope that binds chromatin and supports it is the:
blocks.explanation: On the inner side of the nuclear envelope is a protein lining, the nuclear lamina, which binds chromatin for structural support (3.4).

book_ref.quote: there is a protein lining, called nuclear lamina

blocks.prompt: 61 The subunit of the nuclear pore complex that anchors the pore complex into the nuclear envelope is the:
blocks.explanation: Annular surrounds the inside of the pore, column makes the wall, ring is attached outside the column, lumenal anchors the complex (3.4).

book_ref.quote: lumenal subunit (anchoring the pore complex into the nuclear envelope)

blocks.prompt: 62 Nucleoli are formed at certain sites in chromosomes called:
blocks.explanation: Nucleoli are formed at Nucleolus Organizer Regions (NORs), whose DNA encodes ribosomal RNA (3.4).

book_ref.quote: called Nucleolus Organizer Regions (NORs)

blocks.prompt: 63 In the nucleolus, the fibrillar components consist of:
blocks.explanation: The granules are already formed ribosomal subunits; the fibrils are raw materials of the subunits, i.e. rRNA and associated proteins (3.4).

book_ref.quote: The fibrils are composed of the raw materials of ribosome subunits

blocks.prompt: 64 The genetically active chromatin involved in transcribing RNA is called:
blocks.explanation: Euchromatin is genetically active; the DNA of heterochromatin is genetically inactive (3.4).

book_ref.quote: Euchromatin is the genetically active chromatin

blocks.prompt: 65 The Indian fern Ophioglossum reticulatum has a chromosome number of:
blocks.explanation: Ophioglossum reticulatum has 1,260 chromosomes, showing that chromosome number does not correlate with complexity (3.4).

book_ref.quote: as in the Indian fern (Ophioglossum reticulatum)

blocks.prompt: 66 The DNA inside the nucleus of every human cell is about 6 feet long and is subdivided into:
blocks.explanation: The 6 feet of DNA is subdivided into 46 individual molecules (each 1.5 inches long), one for each chromosome (3.4).

book_ref.quote: there is a 6 feet long DNA

blocks.prompt: 67 The arms of a chromosome are called:
blocks.explanation: A chromosome is made of arms, called chromatids, and a central point, called centromere (3.4).

book_ref.quote: A chromosome is made of arms, called chromatids

blocks.prompt: 68 The single, highly convoluted lumen of the ER (cisternal space) takes up:

options.text: about 1 percent of the cell's volume
more than 10 percent of the cell's volume
80 percent or more of the cell's volume
exactly half of the cell's volume

blocks.explanation: All cisternae are interconnected into one lumen, the cisternal space, which takes up more than 10 percent of the cell's volume (3.4).

book_ref.quote: It takes up more than 10 percent of the total volume of a cell

blocks.prompt: 69 While processing proteins, the rough ER adds to them chemicals such as:
blocks.explanation: During processing, RER adds other chemicals (e.g. sugars) to proteins and transports them or sends them to the Golgi apparatus (3.4).

book_ref.quote: During processing of proteins, RER adds other chemicals (e.g. sugars) to proteins

blocks.prompt: 70 In muscle cells, the smooth ER triggers muscle contraction by releasing:
blocks.explanation: SER stores calcium and does calcium metabolism; in muscle cells it releases calcium to trigger contractions (3.4).

book_ref.quote: In muscle cells, smooth endoplasmic reticulum releases calcium to trigger muscle contractions

blocks.prompt: 71 Smooth ER is much more extensive in liver cells because liver cells carry out:
blocks.explanation: SER is extensive in cells doing much lipid and carbohydrate metabolism (brain, muscle) or detoxification (liver) (3.4).

book_ref.quote: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum is much more extensive in the cells which do lot of lipid

blocks.prompt: 72 Ribosomes are composed of approximately:
blocks.explanation: Ribosomes are tiny granules of about 60 percent rRNA and 40 percent protein, not bound by a membrane (3.4).

book_ref.quote: composed of approximately 60 percent ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and 40 percent protein

blocks.prompt: 73 The subunits of a eukaryotic 80S ribosome are:
blocks.explanation: The eukaryotic ribosome is 80S with a 40S small and a 60S large subunit; prokaryotes have 70S (30S + 50S) (3.4).

book_ref.quote: The complete ribosome in a eukaryotic cell has a Svedberg value of 80S

blocks.prompt: 74 Svedberg values of the two ribosomal subunits do not add up to that of the complete ribosome because the sedimentation rate depends on:

options.text: size and shape, not simply molecular weight

blocks.explanation: Svedberg values are not additive because the rate of sedimentation depends on size and shape rather than simply molecular weight (3.4).

book_ref.quote: depends upon its size and shape, rather than simply its molecular weight

blocks.prompt: 75 During protein synthesis, the RNA that brings amino acids to the ribosome is:
blocks.explanation: mRNA provides the instructions taken from DNA; tRNA brings amino acids to the ribosome (3.4).

book_ref.quote: Transfer RNA (tRNA) brings amino acids to the ribosome

blocks.prompt: 76 Proteins made by ribosomes bound to the RER are mainly:

options.text: kept for the cell's own internal use

blocks.explanation: Proteins of free ribosomes are for the cell's own use, while proteins of RER-bound ribosomes are transported outside the cell (3.4).

book_ref.quote: The proteins that are synthesized by free ribosomes are for the cell

blocks.prompt: 77 Ribosomes are most abundant in cells active in protein synthesis, such as:
blocks.explanation: Ribosomes are most abundant in cells active in protein synthesis, such as pancreas and brain cells (3.4).

book_ref.quote: such as pancreas and brain cells

blocks.prompt: 78 The infoldings of the inner mitochondrial membrane that increase the surface area are called:
blocks.explanation: The inner membrane is highly convoluted and forms many infoldings, the cristae, which increase the surface area (3.4).

book_ref.quote: forms many infoldings called cristae which increase the surface area

blocks.prompt: 79 The knob-like F-1 particles on the inner surface of the cristae are actually:
blocks.explanation: The F-1 particles extending into the matrix are the enzymes ATP-synthase (3.4).

book_ref.quote: These particles are actually the enzymes called ATP-synthase

blocks.prompt: 80 In a mitochondrion, the enzymes of the Krebs cycle are present in the:
blocks.explanation: Enzymes in the matrix catalyse steps like the Krebs cycle; electron transport chain proteins are on the inner membrane (3.4).

book_ref.quote: Enzymes in the matrix catalyse some of the steps of cellular respiration like Krebs cycle

blocks.prompt: 81 The outer membrane of a mitochondrion:

options.text: is smooth and acts like a sieve

blocks.explanation: The outer membrane is smooth and acts like a sieve, filtering out molecules that are too big (3.4).

book_ref.quote: The outer membrane is smooth and acts like a sieve

blocks.prompt: 82 A mitochondrion contains its own:
blocks.explanation: A mitochondrion has its own circular DNA (like prokaryotes), all kinds of RNA and 70S ribosomes, and replicates independently (3.4).

book_ref.quote: all kinds of RNA and 70S ribosomes

blocks.prompt: 83 On average, the chloroplast density on the surface of a leaf is about:
blocks.explanation: The chloroplast density on a leaf surface is about one-half million per square millimetre (3.4).

book_ref.quote: the chloroplast density on the surface of a leaf is about one-half million per square millimetre

blocks.prompt: 84 The semi-fluid inside the inner membrane of a chloroplast, containing dissolved enzymes, is the:
blocks.explanation: Stroma, inside the inner membrane, contains dissolved enzymes and makes up most of the chloroplast's volume (3.4).

book_ref.quote: A semi-fluid called stroma is present inside the inner membrane

blocks.prompt: 85 Stacks of thylakoids in a chloroplast are called:
blocks.explanation: Many thylakoids form stacks called grana (singular granum) (3.4).

book_ref.quote: Many thylakoids form stacks called grana

blocks.prompt: 86 The non-green compartments that connect two grana are the:
blocks.explanation: The lamellae are non-green compartments connecting two grana (3.4).

book_ref.quote: The lamellae are the non-green compartments that connect two grana

blocks.prompt: 87 The colourless plastids involved in storage are:
blocks.explanation: Leucoplasts are colourless and store materials; chromoplasts are yellow-to-red and colour plant parts (3.4).

book_ref.quote: The colourless leucoplasts are involved in the storage

blocks.prompt: 88 Which statement about the two membranes of a chloroplast is correct?

options.text: The outer membrane is much more permeable than the inner one

blocks.explanation: The outer membrane is much more permeable than the inner layer; the inner membranes fuse to form thylakoids (3.4).

book_ref.quote: The outer membrane is much more permeable than the inner layer

blocks.prompt: 89 A Golgi apparatus usually consists of how many cup-shaped cisternae stacked over each other?
blocks.explanation: Golgi apparatus has five to eight cup-shaped cisternae; some unicellular flagellates may have 60 (3.4).

book_ref.quote: Golgi apparatus consists of five to eight cup-shaped

blocks.prompt: 90 The face of a Golgi stack found near the endoplasmic reticulum is the:
blocks.explanation: The cis face is near the ER and receives vesicles; the trans face is near the plasma membrane (3.4).

book_ref.quote: face is found near the endoplasmic reticulum

blocks.prompt: 91 In plant cells, the Golgi apparatus produces:
blocks.explanation: The Golgi apparatus in plant cells produces pectin and other polysaccharides needed for plant structure and metabolism (3.4).

book_ref.quote: the Golgi apparatus in plant cells produces pectin and other polysaccharides

blocks.prompt: 92 Camillo Golgi first named the structure he observed with his staining technique as:
blocks.explanation: Golgi named it the reticular apparatus and announced it in 1898; the electron microscope later confirmed it as an organelle (3.4).

book_ref.quote: named it as reticular apparatus

blocks.prompt: 93 Lysosomal enzymes become inactive in the cytosol because they need a pH of about:
blocks.explanation: Lysosomal enzymes need an acidic pH of about 4.8; the cytosol is neutral, so even released enzymes are inactive (3.4).

book_ref.quote: These enzymes require acidic environment (of pH of about 4.8)

blocks.prompt: 94 Lysosomes contain about how many different hydrolytic enzymes?
blocks.explanation: Lysosomes have about 40 hydrolytic enzymes, made in the ER and modified in the Golgi apparatus (3.4).

book_ref.quote: Lysosomes have about 40 different hydrolytic enzymes

blocks.prompt: 95 In Pompe's disease, harmful amounts of glycogen accumulate in liver cells because lysosomes lack:
blocks.explanation: In Pompe's disease the lysosome lacks a glycogen-digesting enzyme, so glycogen accumulates in liver cells (3.4).

book_ref.quote: the lysosome lacks a glycogen-digesting enzyme

blocks.prompt: 96 In Tay-Sachs disease, the missing lysosomal enzyme causes accumulation of:

options.text: lipids in the nerve cells of the brain

blocks.explanation: In Tay-Sachs disease a lipid-digesting enzyme is missing; lipids accumulate in brain nerve cells and damage the nervous system (3.4).

book_ref.quote: In Tay-Sachs disease an essential lipid-digesting enzyme is missing

blocks.prompt: 97 The breakdown by lysosomes of cellular materials that have exceeded their lifetime is called:
blocks.explanation: Lysosomes perform autophagy, breaking down old cellular materials into simple compounds reused in the cytoplasm (3.4).

book_ref.quote: the lysosomes perform autophagy

blocks.prompt: 98 When a tadpole develops into a frog, the cells of its tail are destroyed by:
blocks.explanation: Selective cell death in development: the tadpole's tail cells are destroyed by lysosomal enzymes (3.4).

book_ref.quote: the cells of the tail are destroyed by the enzymes of lysosomes

blocks.prompt: 99 Christian de Duve suggested the existence of lysosomes after observing that damaged liver cells release:
blocks.explanation: De Duve saw that liver cells damaged in a centrifuge release acid phosphatase and proposed it was held in a membrane-bound organelle (3.4). The book's 'mid-18th century' is a misprint for the mid-20th century.

book_ref.quote: He observed that when cells are damaged in the centrifuge

blocks.prompt: 100 The enzyme catalase in some peroxisomes breaks down hydrogen peroxide into:
blocks.explanation: Catalase breaks hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂ (3.4).

book_ref.quote: which break down hydrogen peroxide (a common by-product of cellular metabolism) into water and oxygen

blocks.prompt: 101 Zellweger syndrome, a congenital disorder, is characterized by:

options.text: absence or reduced number of peroxisomes

blocks.explanation: Zellweger syndrome, the most serious peroxisome disorder, has absent or few peroxisomes and usually causes death in the first year (3.4).

book_ref.quote: The most serious of these disorders is Zellweger syndrome

blocks.prompt: 102 Peroxisomes in liver cells detoxify alcohol by carrying out its:
blocks.explanation: Peroxisome enzymes are mostly oxidative (remove electrons and hydrogens); liver peroxisomes detoxify alcohol by oxidation (3.4).

book_ref.quote: detoxify alcohol and other harmful compounds

blocks.prompt: 103 Glyoxysomes are most abundant in the cells of:

options.text: lipid-rich seeds such as castor beans and soyabeans

blocks.explanation: Glyoxysomes, found only in plant cells, are most abundant in lipid-rich seeds and convert stored lipids into carbohydrates during germination (3.4).

book_ref.quote: They are most abundant in the cells of lipid-rich seeds

blocks.prompt: 104 The membrane enclosing the central vacuole of a plant cell is the:
blocks.explanation: The vacuole is enclosed by the tonoplast; the material inside is cell sap (3.4).

book_ref.quote: The vacuole in plant cells is enclosed by a membrane called tonoplast

blocks.prompt: 105 The large central vacuole of many plant cells takes up:

options.text: 80 percent or more of the cell's space
about 10 percent of the cell's space

blocks.explanation: The central vacuole forms by fusion of smaller vacuoles and takes up most of the cell's space (80 percent or more) (3.4).

book_ref.quote: It takes up most of the space in the cell (80 percent or more)

blocks.prompt: 106 Which of these materials, useful to humans, are stored in plant vacuoles?
blocks.explanation: Materials stored in plant vacuoles that are useful to humans include opium, rubber and garlic flavouring (3.4).

book_ref.quote: such as opium, rubber, and garlic flavouring

blocks.prompt: 107 The two centrioles of a pair are located near the nuclear envelope:

options.text: at right angles to one another
on opposite sides of the cell wall

blocks.explanation: In eukaryotic cells centrioles occur in pairs located at right angles to one another near the nuclear envelope (3.4).

book_ref.quote: The two centrioles are located at right angles to one another

blocks.prompt: 108 Which cells lack centrioles and basal bodies?
blocks.explanation: Plant and fungal cells lack centrioles; their microtubules and spindle fibres are organized from cytoplasmic structures (3.4).

book_ref.quote: The cells of plants and fungi lack centrioles and basal bodies

blocks.prompt: 109 Microfilaments are solid rods made of the globular protein:
blocks.explanation: Microfilaments are solid rods of actin; with myosin they help in cellular contraction (3.4).

book_ref.quote: Microfilaments are solid rods made of a globular protein, called actin

blocks.prompt: 110 Each subunit of a microtubule is made of:
blocks.explanation: Microtubules are hollow cylinders whose subunits are made of alpha-tubulin and beta-tubulin (3.4).

book_ref.quote: two different tubulin proteins known as alpha-tubulin and beta-tubulin

blocks.prompt: 111 The most common protein subunit of intermediate filaments is:
blocks.explanation: Intermediate filaments are made of different proteins; vimentin is the most common, and skin cells contain keratin (3.4).

book_ref.quote: the most common type of protein subunit is vimentin

blocks.prompt: 112 The cytoskeleton fibres that serve as highways for the transport of organelles are:
blocks.explanation: Microtubules give shape to the cell, serve as highways for organelle transport and form cilia, flagella and spindle fibres (3.4).

book_ref.quote: They also serve as highways for the transport of organelles

blocks.prompt: 113 In the axoneme of a cilium, the molecules that bridge the gaps between adjacent microtubule doublets are:
blocks.explanation: Dynein molecules around the circumference of the axoneme bridge the gaps between adjacent doublets (3.4).

book_ref.quote: These dynein molecules bridge the gaps between adjacent microtubule doublets

blocks.prompt: 114 Prokaryotic flagella are built from the protein:
blocks.explanation: Prokaryotic flagella have a completely different structure, built from flagellin, without microtubule triplets (3.4, 3.5).

book_ref.quote: Prokaryotic flagella have a completely different structure built from the protein flagellin

blocks.prompt: 115 In humans, cilia in the lining of the trachea:

options.text: sweep mucus and dirt out of the breathing tubes

blocks.explanation: Cilia lining the trachea sweep mucus and dirt out of the breathing tubes (3.4).

book_ref.quote: cilia are found in the lining of the trachea

blocks.prompt: 116 In a prokaryotic cell, the DNA is present in a more-or-less central region called the:
blocks.explanation: A prokaryotic cell lacks a nucleus; its DNA lies in the nucleoid (nucleus-like region) (3.5).

book_ref.quote: more-or-less central region known as nucleoid

blocks.prompt: 117 Most prokaryotic cells range in length from:
blocks.explanation: Most prokaryotic cells are 2 to 8 µm long, about one-tenth of a typical eukaryotic cell (3.5).

book_ref.quote: Most prokaryotic cells range from 2 to 8

blocks.prompt: 118 In bacteria, the extensions used for attachment are called:
blocks.explanation: Bacteria may have a capsule and extensions for attachment called pili (singular pilus) (3.5).

book_ref.quote: may also have extensions for attachment known as pili

blocks.prompt: 119 A prokaryotic cell divides by:
blocks.explanation: Mitosis and meiosis are missing in prokaryotes; the cell divides by direct division (binary fission) (3.5).

book_ref.quote: it divides by direct division (binary fission)

blocks.prompt: 120 According to the table of differences, the size range of eukaryotic cells is:
blocks.explanation: Eukaryotic cells are 10-100 µm and prokaryotic cells 1-10 µm (3.5).

blocks.prompt: 121 Which feature is shared by both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?
blocks.explanation: Both have DNA as genetic material, a plasma membrane and ribosomes (3.5).

book_ref.quote: both have ribosomes for protein synthesis

blocks.prompt: 122 In photosynthetic prokaryotes, chloroplasts are:

options.text: absent; chlorophyll is scattered in the cytoplasm

blocks.explanation: Prokaryotes lack chloroplasts; their chlorophyll is scattered in the cytoplasm (3.5).

book_ref.quote: Absent; chlorophyll scattered in the cytoplasm

blocks.prompt: 123 The ability of cells to respond to stimuli from their environment by producing cellular responses is called:
blocks.explanation: Cell signalling is the ability of cells to respond to stimuli, involving a series of molecular events that lead to a response (3.6).

book_ref.quote: Cell signalling is the ability of cells to respond to stimuli

blocks.prompt: 124 The first step of cell signalling, in which a ligand binds to its receptor, is:
blocks.explanation: Steps: (1) reception, ligand binds receptor; (2) transduction; (3) cellular response (3.6).

book_ref.quote: Cell signalling begins when a signal molecule (ligand) binds to a receptor

blocks.prompt: 125 During signal transduction, a series of interactions forms a signalling cascade that:
blocks.explanation: After the receptor changes shape, a signalling cascade amplifies the signal (3.6).

book_ref.quote: creating a signalling cascade that amplifies the signal

blocks.prompt: 126 Which of these acts as a second messenger in cell signalling?
blocks.explanation: cAMP, calcium ions and inositol triphosphate (IP₃) act as second messengers carrying the signal from the receptor to targets inside (3.6).

book_ref.quote: Small molecules like cAMP (cyclic AMP), calcium ions, and inositol triphosphate

blocks.prompt: 127 Apoptosis, one possible cellular response to a signal, is:
blocks.explanation: Cellular responses include growth, division, differentiation or apoptosis (programmed cell death) (3.6).

book_ref.quote: apoptosis (programmed cell death)

blocks.prompt: 128 Protein or peptide signalling molecules bind to receptors on the plasma membrane because they:

options.text: are lipophilic and diffuse into the nucleus
are too small to be recognized
are water-soluble and cannot pass through the membrane

blocks.explanation: Protein/peptide signals are water-soluble, so they cannot cross the plasma membrane and bind to surface receptors (3.6).

book_ref.quote: Protein or peptide signalling molecules are water-soluble

blocks.prompt: 129 Steroid hormones bind to receptors located:

options.text: on the outer surface of the plasma membrane only

blocks.explanation: Being lipophilic, steroid hormones diffuse through the plasma membrane and bind intracellular receptors in the cytoplasm or nucleus (3.6).

book_ref.quote: Steroid hormones, being lipophilic, can diffuse through the plasma membrane

blocks.prompt: 130 In steroid signalling, the receptor-hormone complex inside the nucleus:

options.text: binds to specific DNA sequences and regulates transcription
opens ion channels in the membrane

blocks.explanation: The complex binds specific DNA sequences in target genes and regulates their transcription, increasing or decreasing specific proteins (3.6).

book_ref.quote: the receptor-hormone complex binds to specific DNA sequences in target genes

blocks.prompt: 131 The membrane transport mechanism that requires no energy input is:
blocks.explanation: Transport mechanisms are passive transport (no energy input) and active transport (uses energy) (3.7).

book_ref.quote: passive transport (which requires no energy input)

blocks.prompt: 132 Diffusion is the net movement of a substance:

options.text: from lower to higher concentration using ATP
only through carrier proteins using ATP
from higher to lower concentration, along the concentration gradient

blocks.explanation: Diffusion is net movement from higher to lower concentration along the gradient; no energy is spent, so it is passive (3.7).

book_ref.quote: from an area of higher concentration to one of lower concentration

blocks.prompt: 133 The rate of facilitated diffusion depends on:

options.text: the amount of ATP in the cell
the number of transport-protein molecules available in the membrane
the thickness of the cell wall

blocks.explanation: The rate of facilitated diffusion depends on how many transport-protein molecules are available in the membrane (3.7).

book_ref.quote: The rate of facilitated diffusion depends on how many transport-protein molecules are available

blocks.prompt: 134 Gated channel proteins open or close in response to stimuli such as:

options.text: voltage changes, ligand binding or mechanical stress

blocks.explanation: Channel proteins can be gated or non-gated; gated channels respond to voltage changes, ligand binding or mechanical stress (3.7).

book_ref.quote: Gated channels open or close in response to specific stimuli

blocks.prompt: 135 Channel proteins that facilitate the rapid transport of water molecules are:
blocks.explanation: Aquaporins are channel proteins that facilitate the rapid transport of water across the membrane (3.7).

book_ref.quote: aquaporins (facilitate the rapid transport of water molecules)

blocks.prompt: 136 Carrier proteins of facilitated diffusion can become saturated. This means:

options.text: they stop working at low temperature
transport reaches a maximum rate when all carriers are occupied

blocks.explanation: Carrier proteins are highly specific and can become saturated: there is a maximum rate when all are occupied (3.7).

book_ref.quote: They can become saturated, meaning there is a maximum rate of transport

blocks.prompt: 137 Simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer typically involves:

options.text: small, nonpolar molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide
charged ions such as Na⁺ and Cl⁻

blocks.explanation: Simple diffusion involves small nonpolar or lipid-soluble molecules; polar or charged molecules use facilitated diffusion (3.7).

book_ref.quote: Typically involves small, nonpolar molecules such as oxygen

blocks.prompt: 138 In osmosis, water always moves from:

options.text: a hypertonic solution to a hypotonic solution
an isotonic solution to a hypertonic solution only with ATP
a hypotonic solution to a hypertonic solution

blocks.explanation: Water moves from the hypotonic solution (lower solute) to the hypertonic solution (higher solute) (3.7).

book_ref.quote: Water always moves from hypotonic solution

blocks.prompt: 139 Two solutions having equal concentrations of solutes are said to be:
blocks.explanation: Tonicity: hypertonic has more solute, hypotonic less, isotonic equal concentrations (3.7).

book_ref.quote: Isotonic solutions have equal concentrations of solutes

blocks.prompt: 140 In reverse osmosis, water is pushed through a semi-permeable membrane:

options.text: from lower to higher solute concentration without pressure
from higher to lower solute concentration by external pressure

blocks.explanation: Reverse osmosis applies external pressure to push water from higher to lower solute concentration, removing salts and impurities (3.7).

book_ref.quote: reverse osmosis applies external pressure to push water through a semi-permeable membrane

blocks.prompt: 141 In a resting nerve cell, the sodium-potassium pump uses ATP to move:

options.text: Na⁺ to the inside and K⁺ to the outside
both Na⁺ and K⁺ to the outside
Na⁺ to the outside and K⁺ to the inside

blocks.explanation: The pump keeps K⁺ high and Na⁺ low inside the cell by actively moving Na⁺ out and K⁺ in (3.7).

book_ref.quote: the pump actively moves Na⁺ to the outside of the cell and K⁺ to the inside of the cell

blocks.prompt: 142 The form of endocytosis in which a cell takes in liquids as droplets is:
blocks.explanation: In phagocytosis the cell takes in solid material; in pinocytosis it takes in liquids as droplets (3.7).

book_ref.quote: in pinocytosis, cell takes in liquids in the form of droplets

blocks.prompt: 143 Liver cells take up low-density lipoproteins (LDLs) from the blood by:
blocks.explanation: Liver cell receptors recognize and take up LDLs (cholesterol carriers) by receptor-mediated endocytosis (3.7).

book_ref.quote: the cells of liver have receptor proteins for cholesterol

blocks.prompt: 144 In exocytosis, the vesicle carrying bulky material:

options.text: fuses with the plasma membrane and releases its contents outside
detaches from the membrane into the cytoplasm

blocks.explanation: In exocytosis the vesicle moves to the plasma membrane, fuses with it and releases its contents to the outside (3.7).

book_ref.quote: The vesicle moves to the plasma membrane and fuses with it

blocks.prompt: 145 Stem cells that can differentiate into all possible cell types, such as the zygote, are:
blocks.explanation: Totipotent cells (zygote and cells of its first few divisions) can differentiate into all possible cell types (3.8).

book_ref.quote: These stem cells can differentiate into all possible cell types

blocks.prompt: 146 Hematopoietic stem cells, which can become red and white blood cells or platelets, are an example of:
blocks.explanation: Multipotent cells differentiate into a closely related family of cells, e.g. hematopoietic stem cells (3.8).

book_ref.quote: the hematopoietic stem cells can become red and white blood cells or platelets

blocks.prompt: 147 Adult lymphoid or myeloid stem cells, which can form a few different cell types, are:
blocks.explanation: Oligopotent cells differentiate into a few different cell types, e.g. adult lymphoid or myeloid stem cells (3.8).

book_ref.quote: adult lymphoid or myeloid stem cells

blocks.prompt: 148 Adult muscle stem cells produce only their own kind of cells, yet are stem cells because they can renew themselves. They are:
blocks.explanation: Unipotent cells produce only cells of their own type but still self-renew, e.g. adult muscle stem cells (3.8).

book_ref.quote: For example, adult muscle stem cells.

blocks.prompt: 149 Embryonic stem cells (ESCs) are derived from:

options.text: the inner cell mass of blastocysts

blocks.explanation: ESCs come from the inner cell mass of blastocysts (early embryos) and are pluripotent (3.8).

book_ref.quote: ESCs are derived from the inner cell mass of blastocysts

blocks.prompt: 150 Adult stem cells, found in bone marrow, fat and blood, are:
blocks.explanation: Adult stem cells are multipotent: they form a limited range of cell types related to their tissue of origin (3.8).

book_ref.quote: such as bone marrow, fat, and blood

blocks.prompt: 151 Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) are generated in the lab by:

options.text: taking the inner cell mass of blastocysts
reprogramming adult somatic cells using specific transcription factors

blocks.explanation: iPSCs are made by reprogramming adult somatic cells to a pluripotent state using specific transcription factors (3.8).

book_ref.quote: by reprogramming adult somatic cells to a pluripotent state

blocks.prompt: 152 Using stem cells to create models of human diseases for drug testing helps by:

options.text: reducing the reliance on animal models
increasing the risk of immune rejection
removing the need for any testing

blocks.explanation: Stem-cell disease models allow more accurate drug testing and reduce reliance on animal models (3.8).

book_ref.quote: reducing the reliance on animal models

blocks.prompt: 153 In regenerative medicine, stem cells are used to treat conditions such as:

options.text: spinal cord injuries, type 1 diabetes and Parkinson's disease

blocks.explanation: Stem cells can repair or replace damaged tissues, so they are used for spinal cord injuries, type 1 diabetes, Parkinson's disease and heart disease (3.8).

book_ref.quote: spinal cord injuries, type 1 diabetes
